title: TOEFL iBT Reading Practice Test 19
instructions: Read each passage carefully and answer all questions. You have 35 minutes. Questions test factual understanding, vocabulary, inference, and the ability to identify main ideas.

passages.title: Memory and Eyewitness Testimony
passages.text:
For over a century, psychologists have investigated the reliability of eyewitness testimony, particularly after cases where innocent people were convicted based largely on witness accounts later proved false. The field emerged as a serious scientific discipline in the 1970s, when cognitive psychologist Elizabeth Loftus demonstrated that human memory is far more reconstructive and malleable than previously believed. Rather than functioning like a video recording, memory is a dynamic process in which new information can inadvertently alter previously stored information, and emotional arousal can distort recall of specific details.

Loftus's groundbreaking research revealed the phenomenon of the misinformation effect — the tendency for exposure to misleading information after an event to distort memory of that event. In classic experiments, witnesses who were asked misleading questions about details they had observed (such as "Did you see the broken headlight?" when the car actually had an intact headlight) frequently incorporated this false information into their memory and later reported seeing things that were never present. This finding fundamentally challenged the assumption that eyewitness accounts represent accurate reproductions of events.

Subsequent research identified numerous factors that compromise eyewitness accuracy. The weapon focus effect demonstrates that when a suspect brandishes a weapon, witnesses focus disproportionately on the weapon rather than the perpetrator's facial features, leading to diminished identification accuracy. Cross-race identification is substantially more difficult and error-prone than same-race identification, a phenomenon exacerbated by the other-race effect, wherein people recognize faces within their own racial or ethnic group more readily than unfamiliar faces from other groups. Stress and emotional arousal, while sometimes enhancing memory for central details, typically impair memory for peripheral information such as clothing or setting.

Conflicting eyewitness accounts at crime scenes are common because witnesses to the same event often construct different memories based on their individual perspectives, prior knowledge, and emotional states during the incident. Furthermore, confidence in an eyewitness's recollection is surprisingly disconnected from accuracy. Research indicates that highly confident witnesses are not necessarily more accurate than those expressing uncertainty, and in some cases, procedurally conducted interviews can artificially inflate a witness's confidence without improving accuracy. This phenomenon is sometimes termed confidence inflation.

These findings have prompted significant reforms in criminal justice systems worldwide. Double-blind lineup procedures, where the officer administering the lineup does not know the suspect's identity, help prevent inadvertent cueing. Sequential lineups, in which suspects are presented one at a time rather than simultaneously, tend to reduce false identifications. Many jurisdictions now require video recording of interrogations to prevent contamination of memory and reduce false confessions. Despite these advances, eyewitness testimony remains a leading cause of wrongful convictions, underlining the importance of continued research into memory's fallibility.

passages.title: The Development of Modern Cities
passages.text:
The rapid urbanization that characterized the nineteenth and twentieth centuries transformed human settlement patterns and created cities vastly different from earlier urban centres. Medieval and ancient cities typically developed organically around a focal point — a market, fortress, or religious site — and grew irregularly as population pressures accumulated. Modern cities, by contrast, were often planned according to rational geometric principles, reflecting Enlightenment ideals about order, efficiency, and human progress. The grid-pattern street layouts of American cities such as New York and San Francisco exemplify this approach, as do the baroque-influenced radial designs of Paris and Washington, D.C., created by urban planners like Georges-Eugène Haussmann and L'Enfant respectively.

Industrialization served as a primary catalyst for urban expansion during the nineteenth century. Factories required access to raw materials, labour pools, and transportation networks, so industrial cities concentrated along rivers, coasts, and emerging railway corridors. Manchester, England, for instance, grew from a town of roughly 25,000 people in 1772 to over 300,000 by 1850, driven almost entirely by cotton textile manufacturing. This explosive growth strained existing infrastructure and created severe public health challenges. Overcrowding, inadequate sanitation, and pollution from factories contributed to epidemic diseases such as cholera, typhus, and tuberculosis that killed thousands annually.

The industrial city's environmental toll prompted the emergence of urban reform movements in the late nineteenth century. Social reformers, including journalists and public health officials, documented the grim conditions of working-class neighbourhoods and advocated for government intervention. These movements resulted in the development of public sanitation systems, clean water supply networks, and eventually the establishment of parks and green spaces within urban areas. Frederick Law Olmsted's design of Central Park in New York (begun in 1858) exemplified a new philosophy: cities required deliberate provision for recreation and nature to promote public health and social cohesion.

The twentieth century witnessed the decentralization of cities as suburban development accelerated, particularly in North America. Automobile ownership, government-subsidised housing loans (such as those provided by the Federal Housing Administration in the United States), and highway construction enabled middle-class populations to move away from dense urban cores. Suburban sprawl had significant consequences: it reduced tax revenue for central cities, concentrated poverty in urban centres, increased dependence on private automobiles and thus transportation emissions, and consumed agricultural land at unprecedented rates. Simultaneously, city centres were revitalised in some locations through gentrification and the development of downtown commercial and cultural districts.

Contemporary urban development increasingly prioritises sustainability and livability. Cities worldwide are investing in public transit systems, cycling infrastructure, green building standards, and urban parks to reduce environmental impacts and improve residents' quality of life. The recognition that urban design profoundly influences public health, social equity, and environmental outcomes has made urban planning a central concern of twenty-first-century governance.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what did Elizabeth Loftus demonstrate about human memory?
questions.correctAnswer: Memory is reconstructive and malleable rather than like a video recording
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states that Loftus 'demonstrated that human memory is far more reconstructive and malleable than previously believed. Rather than functioning like a video recording, memory is a dynamic process.'
options: Memory functions exactly like a video recording
Memory is reconstructive and malleable rather than like a video recording
Memory is most reliable when emotional arousal is high
Memory loss is inevitable in all individuals

questions.prompt: The word 'malleable' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: capable of being changed or shaped
questions.explanation: 'Malleable' describes something that is flexible and can be altered, similar to how soft metal can be shaped.
options: permanent and unchangeable
capable of being changed or shaped
harmful or dangerous
clear and transparent

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, what is the misinformation effect?
questions.correctAnswer: Exposure to misleading information after an event can distort memory of that event
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 defines the misinformation effect as 'the tendency for exposure to misleading information after an event to distort memory of that event.'
options: The tendency to remember emotional events more vividly
The deliberate distortion of eyewitness testimony
Exposure to misleading information after an event can distort memory of that event
The inability to recall details about weapons

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 3 about the weapon focus effect?
questions.correctAnswer: It reduces the reliability of facial identification in crimes where weapons are present
questions.explanation: The passage explains that when a weapon is present, 'witnesses focus disproportionately on the weapon rather than the perpetrator's facial features, leading to diminished identification accuracy.'
options: Weapons are more memorable than faces
It reduces the reliability of facial identification in crimes where weapons are present
Witnesses always fail to identify suspects in armed crimes
Facial features are less important than weapons in memory

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention the other-race effect in paragraph 3?
questions.correctAnswer: To illustrate an additional factor that compromises eyewitness accuracy
questions.explanation: The other-race effect is presented as one of several factors identified by research that diminish eyewitness reliability.
options: To prove that cross-race identification is always inaccurate
To illustrate an additional factor that compromises eyewitness accuracy
To suggest that witnesses of different races have different memory abilities
To argue against hiring witnesses from minority groups

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 3, which of the following is NOT mentioned as a factor affecting eyewitness accuracy?
questions.correctAnswer: The age of the witness
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 discusses weapon focus, cross-race identification, and stress, but does not mention witness age.
options: The presence of a weapon
The racial similarity between witness and suspect
The age of the witness
Stress during the event

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 4, what is the relationship between witness confidence and accuracy?
questions.correctAnswer: Confidence is not reliably connected to accuracy
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 states that 'confidence in an eyewitness's recollection is surprisingly disconnected from accuracy.'
options: Highly confident witnesses are always more accurate
Confidence is not reliably connected to accuracy
Confidence always indicates false memory
Witnesses who are uncertain are never accurate

questions.prompt: The word 'contamination' in paragraph 5 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: corruption or introduction of unwanted elements
questions.explanation: In the context of interrogations, 'contamination of memory' refers to the introduction of false or misleading information that corrupts the witness's recollection.
options: physical pollution
corruption or introduction of unwanted elements
increased clarity
emotional distance

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential information in this sentence: 'Sequential lineups, in which suspects are presented one at a time rather than simultaneously, tend to reduce false identifications.'
questions.correctAnswer: Presenting suspects individually rather than together tends to produce more accurate identifications
questions.explanation: The sentence compares two lineup procedures and notes that presenting suspects sequentially is more effective at reducing errors.
options: Sequential lineups always result in correct identifications
Presenting suspects individually rather than together tends to produce more accurate identifications
Simultaneous lineups are more fair to suspects
Sequential lineups were invented to confuse witnesses

questions.prompt: Complete a summary of the passage. Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas.
questions.correctAnswer: A,C,E
questions.explanation: The passage's main themes are the reconstructive nature of memory (A), the multiple factors that reduce eyewitness reliability (C), and the resulting reforms in criminal justice (E).
options: A. Human memory is reconstructive and subject to distortion from new information and emotional factors.
B. Elizabeth Loftus proved that eyewitness testimony is always completely unreliable.
C. Multiple psychological factors including weapon focus, cross-race identification difficulty, and stress compromise eyewitness accuracy.
D. Video recording of interrogations has eliminated all wrongful convictions.
E. Criminal justice systems have adopted reforms such as double-blind lineups and sequential presentation to reduce reliance on flawed eyewitness accounts.
F. Medieval cities were superior to modern cities because they developed organically.

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 1, what typically served as a focal point for medieval and ancient cities?
questions.correctAnswer: A market, fortress, or religious site
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 states that medieval and ancient cities 'typically developed organically around a focal point — a market, fortress, or religious site.'
options: A factory or industrial zone
A market, fortress, or religious site
A grid-pattern street layout
A government administrative centre

questions.prompt: The word 'organic' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: developing naturally without planned design
questions.explanation: 'Organic growth' refers to development that occurs naturally and gradually, in contrast to planned or designed growth.
options: related to living matter
developing naturally without planned design
geometric and orderly
based on ancient principles

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 2, what was the primary reason for Manchester's growth from 1772 to 1850?
questions.correctAnswer: Cotton textile manufacturing
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that Manchester 'grew from a town of roughly 25,000 people in 1772 to over 300,000 by 1850, driven almost entirely by cotton textile manufacturing.'
options: Immigration and natural population growth
Development of recreational facilities
Cotton textile manufacturing
Government relocation of businesses

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention Frederick Law Olmsted's design of Central Park in paragraph 3?
questions.correctAnswer: To exemplify a new philosophy that cities require deliberate provision for recreation and nature
questions.explanation: Central Park is presented as an example of a new urban philosophy that addresses public health and social cohesion through parks.
options: To show that early industrial cities were well-designed
To exemplify a new philosophy that cities require deliberate provision for recreation and nature
To argue that New York was the first modern city
To illustrate problems caused by industrial pollution

questions.prompt: What can be inferred from paragraph 4 about suburban sprawl in North America?
questions.correctAnswer: Government policies actively encouraged movement away from city centres
questions.explanation: The passage explains that 'government-subsidised housing loans' and 'highway construction enabled middle-class populations to move away from dense urban cores,' indicating government support for sprawl.
options: Suburban sprawl occurred entirely due to individual choice
Government policies actively encouraged movement away from city centres
Automobiles were not important in suburban development
Poverty in central cities decreased as a result of suburban growth

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 4, which of the following was NOT mentioned as a consequence of suburban sprawl?
questions.correctAnswer: Improved air quality in rural areas
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 mentions reduced tax revenue, concentrated poverty, increased emissions, and agricultural land loss, but does not mention air quality improvements.
options: Reduced tax revenue for central cities
Concentration of poverty in urban centres
Increased automobile emissions
Improved air quality in rural areas

questions.prompt: According to paragraph 5, what contemporary urban development priorities are mentioned?
questions.correctAnswer: Public transit, cycling infrastructure, green building standards, and urban parks
questions.explanation: Paragraph 5 states that cities are 'investing in public transit systems, cycling infrastructure, green building standards, and urban parks.'
options: Factories and manufacturing zones
Public transit, cycling infrastructure, green building standards, and urban parks
Residential sprawl and highway expansion
Commercial development only

questions.prompt: The word 'revitalised' in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to:
questions.correctAnswer: brought back to vigour or renewed
questions.explanation: 'Revitalised' means restored to health, energy, or prosperity after decline.
options: completely destroyed
brought back to vigour or renewed
abandoned permanently
forgotten by residents

questions.prompt: Which best expresses the essential information in this sentence: 'Medieval and ancient cities typically developed organically around a focal point — a market, fortress, or religious site — and grew irregularly as population pressures accumulated.'
questions.correctAnswer: Early cities developed gradually around a central location and expanded unevenly with population growth
questions.explanation: The sentence describes unplanned growth concentrated around a focal point that changed as population increased.
options: Medieval cities were always built according to geometric plans
Early cities developed gradually around a central location and expanded unevenly with population growth
Markets were always the most important part of ancient cities
Population growth had no effect on city development

questions.prompt: Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas in the passage.
questions.correctAnswer: B,D,F
questions.explanation: The passage emphasises the contrast between organic and planned city development (B), industrialisation as a driver of urbanisation (D), and contemporary emphasis on sustainability (F).
options: A. Grid-pattern streets are superior to all other urban designs.
B. Modern cities developed according to rational geometric plans, contrasting with the organic growth of medieval and ancient cities.
C. Central Park was the first park ever built in a city.
D. Industrialisation concentrated cities along rivers, coasts, and railways, leading to rapid growth and public health challenges.
E. Suburban development has eliminated poverty in modern cities.
F. Contemporary urban planning prioritises sustainability and livability through transit, cycling infrastructure, green buildings, and parks.
